title: Social Studies: Past and Present
objectives: I can explain what ten words about history and communities mean.
I can use these words to tell how a town begins and how people remember its past.
I can use the endings -ment and -ant to understand new words.
I can write about my own family or community using words from this unit.
rationale: These are the words history texts assume students already know. Three are Tier 3 social studies terms (colony, immigrant, government) and seven are Tier 2 words that carry history reading in grades 4 to 6 (ancestor, culture, frontier, settlement, descendant, ceremony, homeland). The unit builds one story from beginning to end: people leave a homeland, cross to a colony, reach the frontier, build a settlement, form a government, and later hold a ceremony to honor their culture and ancestors. Students use the exploration words from unit 4 (voyage, expedition, caravan) as the way these people arrived, and the endings -ment and -ant give a small word-study strand.

passage.title: Maple Hollow Remembers
paras: More than two hundred years ago, a small group of families left their homeland across the sea and sailed to a new colony on the coast. They were immigrants, and they hoped for farmland and a fresh start. Many carried only a trunk of clothes, a few tools, and old family recipes.

The families traveled inland until they reached the edge of the frontier, where few towns existed. There they built a settlement and named it Maple Hollow. Houses went up first, then a meeting hall. The settlers voted on rules together, and those rules became the town's first government.

Each fall, the descendants of those families gather for a ceremony in the town square. They read the names of their ancestors and share foods from the old country. The celebration keeps their culture alive for the children of today.

Visitors to the Maple Hollow museum can see a map of the homeland the families left, along with letters, tools, and a worn wooden trunk. The past is not far away in this town, because every year the people remember it together.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, what does the word "frontier" mean?
choices: The edge of settled land where few people live
The middle of a busy city
A kind of wooden house
A river in the colony
qs.why: The families traveled until they reached a place where few towns existed, which is the frontier.

qs.q: Why does the passage call the families "immigrants"?
choices: They sold goods in a market.
They were visiting the coast for a day.
They wanted to build a museum.
They moved from their homeland to live in a new place.
qs.why: They left their homeland and sailed to a new colony to live there.

qs.q: What does the yearly ceremony tell you about the people of Maple Hollow?
choices: They are tired of old stories.
They want to forget the families who started the town.
They care about remembering their ancestors and culture.
They plan to move away soon.
qs.why: They read ancestors' names and share old foods, which shows they value their past.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the first settlers made rules together?
choices: They carried a trunk of clothes.
They built houses first and a meeting hall next.
They voted on rules that became the town's first government.
They traveled inland from the coast.
qs.why: Voting on rules together is how the first government began.

qs.q: Which statement best tells the main idea?
choices: Families who settled a town still remember their past through shared events.
Maple Hollow is the biggest town in the country.
Ships were the only way to travel long ago.
Farmland is more useful than a museum.
qs.why: The passage follows the families from arrival to a ceremony and museum that keep their story alive.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten social studies words by following one story, from leaving a homeland to remembering the past in a ceremony. The unit connects to the exploration words of unit 4 and gives a short word-study strand on -ment and -ant.

notes.va.colony.n: Taught with the history sense: a place ruled by a faraway country. Mention the animal sense, a colony of ants, so students know the word has two uses. Show the colonies on a map before reading.
notes.va.immigrant.n: Distinguish from tourist and from visitor. Make sure the class talks about immigrants with respect; many students may have immigrant families. Link to the prefix im-, a spelling of in-.
notes.va.government.n: Use a class example: who decides what? Students often think the government is only one person. Show govern + -ment, the result of ruling.
notes.va.ancestor.n: Pair with descendant. Draw a line with ancestor on the left and descendant on the right to show the order in time.
notes.va.culture.n: Culture is not only food and holidays; it includes language, stories, and values. Give students a chance to name something from their own culture, but never require it.
notes.va.frontier.n: In history texts, the frontier is the edge of settled land; be aware the term was used in a way that ignores the people already living there. Mention that Native peoples lived on these lands.
notes.va.settlement.n: Settle + -ment. Ask what a place needs before it is a settlement: homes, water, food, and people willing to stay.
notes.va.descendant.n: The root idea is a line going down: ancestors above, descendants below. Students often reverse the pair; use the family tree picture.
notes.va.ceremony.n: A ceremony has set actions that people repeat. Contrast with a party. Ask students for a ceremony in school, such as an assembly.
notes.va.homeland.n: A compound of home and land. Use with care: for some students the homeland is not a single country or may be a place they have never lived. Offer choices when they write.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says families left their homeland and sailed to a colony. Homeland is home plus land, the place they came from. A colony is a place ruled by a faraway country, so the settlers were also immigrants. I can see how the words connect in one story.'

needsReview: Spanish glosses (colonia, inmigrante, gobierno, antepasado, cultura, frontera, asentamiento, descendiente, ceremonia, patria) not reviewed by a native speaker; frontera is often border, so check the sense for frontier.
Maple Hollow is an invented town; the first paragraph's timing and the voyage are plausible but not tied to a real event.
Frontier carries a settler viewpoint; teacher note adds a caution about Native peoples. A person should review the framing.
The Virginia example in the colony sentence is a real fact: Virginia was an English colony before the United States existed.
